candidates.teaser: The world's most recognized drink wasn't always the color you think — and the reason it changed is stranger than you'd expect.
candidates.video_description: Before it became the iconic caramel-brown liquid the world knows, Coca-Cola was a completely different color. The change wasn't accidental — it was a deliberate decision tied to a surprising problem. Most people have been looking at a myth their entire lives.
candidates.script: Coca-Cola was never supposed to be brown. The original formula produced a bright green liquid — but it was dyed caramel to hide the inconsistent batches that looked different bottle to bottle. The company chose a uniform color over transparency, literally. So every time you crack open a Coke, you're drinking a product whose entire iconic look exists to conceal imperfection. Does that change how it tastes to you?

candidates.teaser: There's a creature alive today that was swimming the oceans before a single tree existed on Earth — and you've probably seen one at an aquarium.
candidates.video_title: Sharks Are Older Than Trees — Let That Sink In
candidates.video_description: Sharks have existed for over 450 million years, making them older than trees, which only appeared around 350 million years ago. They survived every mass extinction event that wiped out the dominant life of each era. Whatever ended the dinosaurs didn't even slow them down.
candidates.script: Sharks are older than trees. Not a little older — sharks were already 100 million years into their existence when the first tree grew on land. They survived five mass extinctions, including the one that erased the dinosaurs. Their design was so perfect that evolution barely touched them in 450 million years. Meanwhile, trees showed up late, and we still nearly lost the sharks. So who's actually the more advanced species here?

candidates.teaser: There's a bell ringing inside a glass case at Oxford that hasn't stopped since before your great-great-grandparents were born — and no one can open it to find out why.
candidates.video_title: This Bell Has Been Ringing Since 1840
candidates.video_description: The Oxford Electric Bell has been ringing almost continuously since 1840, powered by a dry pile battery whose composition remains unknown because opening the case would stop the experiment. It has rung an estimated 10 billion times. The battery should have died over a century ago.
candidates.script: There is a bell at Oxford University that has been ringing since 1840 — that's over 184 years without stopping. It's powered by a dry pile battery no one has ever opened, because cracking the case would end the experiment forever. It has rung approximately 10 billion times. Scientists know it works. They just don't know exactly why it hasn't died. The world's longest-running experiment, and we're too afraid to look inside.

candidates.topic: Neil Armstrong's Heartbeat on the Moon
candidates.teaser: When Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon, NASA's doctors monitoring from Earth were more scared than he was — and his heartbeat proved it.
candidates.video_title: Neil Armstrong's Heart Nearly Stopped on the Moon
candidates.video_description: As Neil Armstrong descended the ladder onto the lunar surface in 1969, NASA flight surgeons recorded his heart rate spiking to 150 beats per minute — double his resting rate. The moment one human foot touched the Moon, the steadiest man in the room was the one in the spacesuit. Armstrong himself later said it was simply excitement.
candidates.script: The moment Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon in 1969, NASA doctors watching from Earth saw his heart rate explode to 150 beats per minute. The man who trained for years, who flew combat missions in Korea, who nearly died in a lunar module simulation — his heart was pounding like he'd just sprinted. He later said it was pure excitement. But mission control had their fingers hovering over the abort switch the entire time. Coolest man alive, or just the best at hiding fear?

candidates.topic: The Density of a Neutron Star
candidates.teaser: A single teaspoon of something in deep space weighs more than every car, building, and human being on Earth combined — and it fits in your kitchen.
candidates.video_title: A Teaspoon of This Weighs More Than Earth's Oceans
candidates.video_description: Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of massive stars, so dense that a single teaspoon of their material would weigh approximately one billion tons on Earth. They are roughly 20 kilometers in diameter yet contain more mass than our Sun. Gravity on their surface is 200 billion times stronger than what you feel right now.
candidates.script: One teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh one billion tons on Earth. The entire object is only 20 kilometers wide — smaller than most cities — yet it contains more mass than our Sun. Gravity on its surface is 200 billion times stronger than what's holding you to the ground right now. These things are spinning up to 700 times per second. The universe built something city-sized that outweighs entire solar systems. And there are billions of them out there.
